title: The Opposing Good
logline: A person who once did real harm now spends every day doing quiet, repeated service at a community kitchen, without ever explaining why to the people they serve.

object.note: Object 8 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: From forces no one can bargain with to one person's steady daily service, a quiet answer to something done long before.

thread_out.thread: Work that answers for the past leads to a family walking the land a father left, where every fence post seems to remember something different.

requirements: A community kitchen or shelter with a long-term volunteer willing to be filmed and to control their own story
Full consent over what personal history, if any, is disclosed

lesson.in_simple_terms: The texts teach that no single act has the last word: later actions can strengthen or weaken earlier ones, and someone who has done harm is advised to take up the opposite good.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: එක් ක්‍රියාවක් අවසාන තීරණය නොවන බවත්, පසුව කරන ක්‍රියා මගින් පෙර කළ දේවල බලය වැඩි හෝ අඩු විය හැකි බවත්, වරදක් කළ කෙනෙකු එයට විරුද්ධ යහපත කළ යුතු බවත් ධර්මය කියයි.
lesson.the_teaching: The Abhidhamma defines kamma as intention (cetanā) and describes four jobs an action can do: produce a result, support it, obstruct it, or cut it off. The Margaya says these are not separate kinds of action but roles that actions play, that a weak action can be strengthened by later ones and a strong one weakened by later opposing actions, and so it advises those who have done wrong to do the good that opposes it. The texts also map harm in ten courses, three of body, four of speech and three of mind, so that harm has a shape and a weight.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The film stays with the work itself: chopping, serving, wiping tables, the same tasks on different days, done with a steadiness that becomes its own statement. The person's past is never narrated for them. From the repetition and from their care with the people they serve, the viewer senses that this is an answer to something, and is left to feel how steady good can press against what came before.
lesson.caution: This is not a ledger in which good and bad cancel out, and it does not mean anyone's suffering was deserved: the texts describe stronger forces overriding weaker ones, not a sum or a sentence.
lesson.builds_on: The last film faced forces no one can bargain with; this one turns to what a person can still do, adding that later good can weaken the force of earlier harm.
